title: FontLab Blog
description: News, technical writing, and updates from FontLab.

items.title: Introducing FontLab 9
items.content_html:
FontLab 9 for Mac and Windows is now available. Revolutionary stem editing. Ultrasmooth tangents. Curved interpolation. Bracket layers. Optical oblique. Neural spacing & kerning. Visual features. AI, MCP & UI in 19 languages. Buy lifetime: $499. Upgrade from FontLab: $149, $49 or free!.

Ask Aidus, FontLab’s built-in assistant powered by a large language model of your choice, anything: ask it about the app, about the current font. Ask it to build Font window filters, to write simple Python scripts, to write proof texts. Create a new glyph with Aidus using context-aware image generation.

Adjust the weight, width and slope of stems across one or several glyphs with the new Stem tool: visually, by units or by percentage. View Thickness consistency along curved and diagonal stems with Quick measurement rainbow.

Draw more confidently with the improved Pen tool: preview the next segment, draw corners, curves and tangents, or refine existing handles. Draw live calligraphic strokes with new Power Brush: use the Thickness tool to change the brush thickness, angle and roundness for every node. Add variation-compatible ink traps.

Ensure perfect G2-smoothness with Genius Tangent nodes when a line segment transitions to curve, and on rounded Smart Corners. Simplify part of a contour with the new Trowel tool, or clear an area with the Cleaner tool. Turn bitmap images into contours more accurately with improved Autotrace.

Turn on Quick Preview on drag and focus on the shape whenenver you drag: all the distractions disappear. Turn all snapping on and off at once with Enable Snapping. Repeat the last command on a different glyph or layer with Repeat.

Interpolate along curves with the Sigma tool. Switch construction partway along the axis with bracket layers. Slant glyphs with Make oblique action that performs automatic optical adjustment.

Kern existing and planned pairs in the new Superkerning panel. Use one set of kerning classes in all masters. Auto Space and Auto Kern with new neural algorithms. Preview multiple font sizes, masters, instances in the new Notepad panel; build and edit specimens, and export then to PDF.

Selectively copy-paste contours, appearance, metrics, anchors, guides, hints or masks across masters with Paste Special. Reuse Skin elements. Reshape elements with the Mesh filter. See which glyphs have contours, components or advanced elements with Color-code element type.

Visually edit and test features for all writing systems in the Lookups editor, test with the step-by-step lookup debugger. Control ligature caret positioning with anchors. Export visual TrueType hints into static and variable fonts with the genuine VTT engine.

Open and export Glyphs 4 files. Import Open Font Format 2026 fonts with cubic TrueType outlines, variable components and avar version 2 mappings. Automate your work with improved Python scripting. Automate FontLab from external scripts and agents with the built-in MCP server.

Use the interface and built-in help in 19 languages: English, Deutsch, Français, Español, Polski, Čeština, हिन्दी, Bahasa Indonesia, Italiano, 日本語, 한국어, Português, Русский, ไทย, Türkçe, Українська, Tiếng Việt, 简体中文, 繁體中文. Learn FontLab 9 from the all-new user manual. Simplify the user interface with Focused Menu.

items.title: FontLab Pad 2.1: free typesetting app that lets you use every font and every glyph
items.content_html: FontLab Pad 2.1 adds OpenType feature controls and other improvements. And it’s still free for Mac and Windows!

items.title: FontLab Pad 2: get the look you want, then paste it where you need it
items.content_html: You found a font you love, and your app is showing you a fraction of it. With FontLab Pad 2 you try the font without installing it, set your headline exactly the way you want it, and paste the result into whatever you are working in. Pad has been free for ten years, and it still is!

items.title: TransType 5: every style of your variable fonts, in every app
items.content_html: Your variable font holds hundreds of styles. Word shows you nine. Some apps show you one. Drop it into TransType 5, add any instance you want, click Convert: every style lands in your font menus, ready to use. 10 conversions are free!

items.title: Make your pixels vexy. Play with lines.
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front .illu-photo }

Vexy Playlines turns any photo into vector art in the browser: drop an image, pick one of fourteen algorithmic fills, from classic linear or dotted halftones, to stipple, low-poly, wireframe, ASCII. Drag a slider or two, export SVG! Five fills are free with no sign-up, nothing to install; nine more unlock with a FontLab Pass. Try the quick little cousin of our Mac and Windows Vexy Lines app — built for the ten-minute detour that eats an afternoon.

items.title: Poor print produces pretty posters
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front .illu-photo }

In 1977, Albert Kapr squeezed poster style out of cheap GDR paper and a one-colour press. The Vexy Lines case study: retro poster scans his SC Dynamo sheet, rebuilds the halftone photo into a vector signal where stroke thickness answers to luminance, and pours one photograph into three posters: faithful linear, colour-soaked, and full brutalist for the scrolling feed.

items.title: Your gradient will not survive the vinyl cutter
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front .illu-photo }

Airbrushed lettering dies at the vinyl cutter: no edge to follow, no colour to separate. The Vexy Lines case study: lettering rebuilds the glow as flat vector structure: halftone stars sized by brightness, masked outlines, hand-tuned Béziers. The result cuts cleanly at 2 meters, separates to spot colours, and stays editable the whole way.

items.title: Your face on your next crypto banknotes
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front .illu-photo }

Many headshots, many cameras, one team photoshoot: with Vexy Lines, you can turn low-quality photos into visually harmonized, crisp SVGs & PDFs. Turn your starship crew into WSJ-style hedcuts or brutalist stipples, and showcase them from avatar to hero. This look is worth every penny!

items.title: Type that reads the picture underneath it
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front }

With Vexy Lines, you can make the most of your variable fonts. Create expressive typographic arrangements, impactful headlines and font specimens. Check out the Vexy Lines case study: Text fill! It typesets your text along the baselines created by the app’s procedural patterns. Each text glyph picks its font size or variable font instance from the brightness of the image beneath it. Sampled per glyph. Mapped to Weight, Width, Optical Size, or any other axis. Exported to SVG & PDF. For foundries who want to show their design spaces flow along pixels.

items.title: A new home for Vexy Lines where pixels become lines
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-front .illu-photo }

In October 2025, we launched Vexy Lines, a Mac & Windows app that redraws any photo as editable vector line art: engraving, halftone, stipple, wireframe, even live variable type that reads the image beneath it. We just revamped the vexy.art/lines website, which now includes real-life case studies.

items.title: Vexy Lines 2 is here!
items.content_html: Say hello to Vexy Lines 2, with all-new image filters, a stroke-cutting sharp mask, cross-hatching diamond dots, organic wobble & rough strokes, much faster parameter tweaking, and hundreds of other improvements. If you have Vexy Lines 1, it’s free!

items.title: FontLab TV: 50-hour variable font course now available
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

FontLab TV has published a 50-hour video course on variable font design, organized into 25 playlists. It runs from absolute fundamentals — coordinates, contours, metrics — through production, hinting, export, and font business basics.

items.title: From bland to bold: turning any image into a vector with Vexy Lines
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

A photograph is not a vector. A sketch is not a vector. A scanned logo is definitely not a vector. Vexy Lines exists to fix that, one image at a time.

items.title: Color fonts in 2026: COLR v1, SVG, sbix, and bitmap strikes
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

In 2013, color OpenType looked like a standards argument with four exits. Apple had sbix. Google had CBDT/CBLC. Microsoft had COLR/CPAL. Adobe and Mozilla had SVG-in-OpenType. The question then was which proposal would win. In 2026, the answer is less tidy and more useful: they all became real OpenType color font formats, but they did not become equally useful everywhere.

items.title: The hedcut at 45
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

In 1979, a Wall Street Journal illustrator named Kevin Sprouls introduced a stipple portrait to the paper. Forty-five years later, the same form is still running on the front page. That is unusual enough to warrant an explanation.

items.title: The old fonts are not dead — they are just waiting in a folder
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

Nothing gets old faster than a font format — until a client opens a twenty-year-old file and suddenly it is everybody’s problem again.

items.title: From Spirograph to Fidenza
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

The generative line has a genealogy. It runs from a physics lecture in 1815 through a children’s toy in 1965 and a university lab in 2001, and it ends — so far — with an algorithm that sold for five million dollars.

items.title: Money lace — guilloché, intaglio, and the Spirograph
items.content_html:
{ .illu-thumb .illu-index }

The fine-line patterns on a banknote are a security feature. A British engineer made a toy of them in 1965 and sold 30 million units.

items.title: Made with FontLab: Fábio Duarte Martins
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

Scannerlicker is Fábio Duarte Martins’s foundry, and his testimonial is one of the few that actually names the FontLab features doing the work. It is, accidentally, a short manual on what to learn first.

items.title: Sister Corita Kent, the silkscreen nun
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

Frances Kent took her students to see Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup show, came back to Immaculate Heart College, and turned supermarket packaging into devotional art.

items.title: Drawing the invisible — contour lines and Minard
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

A contour line is a lie your map tells you so you can understand the truth. No hill has a line around it. The line is what you draw when the hill refuses to fit on a flat page.

items.title: Warhol's August 1962 silkscreen pivot
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

Andy Warhol started screenprinting in August 1962. His explanation: “I wanted something stronger that gave more of an assembly line effect.”

items.title: Five centuries of line — Dürer, Hogarth, Bewick, Doré
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

A line can carry tone, texture, shadow, and emotion — and never once pretend to be a photograph. That is the whole argument of five centuries of printmaking, made with a burin, a graver, and eventually a stylus.

items.title: Dithering, ditherpunk, and Bill Atkinson
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

A one-bit display has no grey. Dithering is the sixty-year argument that it doesn’t need one.

items.title: Seurat and the 220,000 dots
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

Georges Seurat spent two years applying roughly 220,000 dots to a canvas. The painting works because the dots don’t blend on the canvas. They blend in your eye.

items.title: Halftone, from Fox Talbot to A Scene in Shantytown
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

Photography arrived in the 1830s. Printing photographs in newspapers took another fifty years.

items.title: Variable fonts in motion and interface
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

Typography on screen used to mean “pick a weight and hope for the best.” Now the weight can follow the user.

items.title: GSUB, GPOS, and HarfBuzz: the machinery under OpenType
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

Every OpenType feature — ligatures, kerning, small caps, Arabic joining forms — runs through two tables and one engine. Most type designers know the features exist. Fewer know what the tables look like from the inside.

items.title: Made with FontLab: Yuri Gordon
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb }

Acqua Aldina is a variable serif drawn by hand. Baker Street 221B is a three-font Sherlockian set with a font for the detective, the doctor, and the housekeeper. Yuri Gordon’s catalogue does not pretend to fit one mood, and he’s open about why FontLab works for the spread.

items.title: The four-stack of screen rendering
items.content_html:
{.illu-thumb .illu-index}

Most type designers know their fonts will be rendered differently on macOS and Windows. Fewer know the names of the four pieces of plumbing responsible. The names are worth knowing, because the plumbing shapes everything.
